rationale: A wins because it does the strategist's job: it finds several real story shapes and refuses the fake customer story instead of laundering a missing asset into an angle. A's "Deel's AI Will Flag Your Contractor Risk Across 150 Countries. It Won't Tell You If It's Right." is the cleanest, best-grounded story in the pile. B has muscle in "A $12B payroll company just made AI compliance a free feature, not a product," but then keeps "One employer, one bad contractor call" with no employer. That's not restraint; that's a placeholder in a suit.
gaps_in_A: "Deel's launch is the first concrete product the reporter can point to as evidence of the shift" invents a category claim the update does not support. Deel is a concrete example, not proof it is first or that the market moved.
"Global Compliance Used to Happen After the Hire" asserts a before-state not in the supplied facts. The update only says this tool checks risk as a company hires.
"competitive pressure driving the launch" is a good question but still speculative without lawsuit timing or product-development chronology.

"Moat Over Margin" is plausible business analysis, but it jumps from "included for existing customers" to a monetization thesis before proving whether the inclusion is permanent or how new customers pay.
gaps_in_B: "One employer, one bad contractor call" should have been refused, not kept. The set admits "Without a named customer there is no story at this rung" and then pitches the rung anyway.
"while defending itself in a corporate-espionage lawsuit" invents litigation posture. The update only says Deel is in a lawsuit with a competitor.
"automating that call" and "when the tool clears a worker" overstate the product. The facts say it flags risks, not that it makes or clears classification decisions.
"rather than selling a new SKU" is not supplied. "Included for existing customers" does not prove the new-customer packaging or permanent pricing model.
